title: An Empirical Study of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs

paper.title: An Empirical Study of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
paper.abstract:
Abstract Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods are critical for adapting large models under resource-constrained settings. However, as mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, which offer efficient inference at massive parameter scales, gain increasing prevalence in the community, a critical gap arising from the lack of systematic recipes for applying PEFT to MoE models. To narrow this gap, we conduct a large-scale systematic study that investigates a set of essential design recipes, including which modules should be adapted, which granularity should be used to adapt MoE modules, which PEFT method to use, and to what extent should the load-balancing objective be used, across three MoE backbones on downstream tasks and general knowledge tasks. Our experiments yield several key insights. First, adapting MoE experts alone achieves the highest downstream performance with competitive general capability retention under a comparable parameter budget. Second, native expert-weight updates offer a better downstream–retention trade-off than adapters that bypass experts or entire MoE modules. Third, LoRA and DoRA together define the strongest operating region for high downstream accuracy among the evaluated PEFT methods. Fourth, no nonzero load-balancing coefficient Pareto-dominates the zero baseline.
We finally evaluate a weight-level redesign of MoE 2 -LoRA on Qwen3. Moving its module-level bypass pool into native expert weights
improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters and a 3.2-point average downstream cost.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Mixture-of-experts architectures ( Shazeer et al., 2017 ; Lepikhin et al., 2021 ; Fedus et al., 2022 ; Du et al., 2022 ) enable extensive scaling of model parameters while activating only a small fraction of parameters per input unit. This sparse activation paradigm offers an outstanding trade-off between performance and computation, and has consequently been adopted by frontier models such as GLM-5.2 ( GLM-5 Team, 2026 ) and Kimi-K3 ( Kimi Team, 2026 ) . Despite the increasing prevalence of MoE architectures, most existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Houlsby et al., 2019 ; Li and Liang, 2021 ) and recipes were originally designed for dense models, and the community still lacks a systematic guideline for applying PEFT methods to MoE structures. Given that MoE models typically comprise a massive number of parameters, it is essential to adopt a scientifically grounded guideline for applying PEFT to such models to achieve efficient adaptation. This gap therefore raises a pressing question: How can we adapt MoE models to achieve the best performance-efficiency balance with the least forgetting? To answer this question, we conduct a large-scale systematic empirical study using representative MoE backbones from different families, including Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) , Gemma-4-26B-A4B ( Gemma Team, 2026 ) , and GPT-OSS-20B ( OpenAI, 2025 ) . Specifically, we structure our study around four main axes: (1) which modules should be targeted for adapting MoE models under a similar trainable parameter budget? (2) should adaptation granularity for MoE modules be set at the module level, expert level, or weight level? (3) which PEFT method generally works best for adapting MoE models? (4) how strong should the auxiliary loss coefficient be set for adapting MoE models? We conduct the study using two distinct downstream tasks and two general tasks. The first downstream task is mathematical reasoning, on which base models typically already possess strong capabilities; it serves to probe whether further leverages well-established knowledge. The second downstream task is an intent classification task, which yields unsatisfactory results for the three base models and therefore provides a more stringent test of a PEFT method’s ability to adapt in under-represented regimes. Our study therefore yields four instructive insights: (1) applying adaptation solely to experts, achieves the best downstream performance; (2) within the MoE modules, applying adaptation at the weight level is more reliable than at the expert level or module level; (3) among the evaluated PEFT methods, LoRA and DoRA deliver the strongest downstream performance, whereas methods with weaker general capabilities retention can fail to learn the target task properly; (4) auxiliary load balancing may degrade performance on both downstream tasks and general capabilities retention. Guided by these findings, we revisit MoE 2 -LoRA, a PEFT method tailred for MoE fine-tuning, which established a learned mapping between the selection of pre-trained MoE experts and that of LoRA experts. Our modification on MoE 2 -LoRA improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters and only a 3.2-point average downstream cost, turning a large task-dependent forgetting into near-complete retention and thereby showing that our insights are effective beyond the controlled grid. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • To our knowledge, this is the first large-scale PEFT study conducted directly on pretrained MoE LLMs, covering four design axes, three heterogeneous backbones, and two downstream tasks. Beyond the downstream accuracy that PEFT work usually reports alone, we pair every selected checkpoint with general-capability evaluation on MMLU-Pro and IFEval, so each design choice is judged by what it gains and by what it costs the pretrained model. • We distill the study into four actionable insights on adaptation position, expert granularity, update form, and load balancing, each stated with the regime in which it holds, providing concrete defaults and open questions for future work on MoE adaptation. Functional and spectral analyses explain how weight-level updates reuse pretrained expert computation. • We show the insights are practical by refining MoE 2 -LoRA, a recent routed-pool method, along the single axis it does not already follow, which improves all four general-capability endpoints with 17% fewer parameters.

sections.heading: Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning (PEFT).
sections.text: PEFT adapts large models by learning a small set of parameters while keeping pretrained weights largely frozen. Low-rank methods modify pretrained weights through compact updates: LoRA learns a low-rank residual, while DoRA decouples weight magnitude and direction to improve the update ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2024a ) . OFT and FourierFT further restrict the update space through orthogonal transformations and frequency-domain parameterization, respectively ( Qiu et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2024b ) , whereas IA3 adapts the model by scaling intermediate activations ( Liu et al., 2022 ) . A complementary line introduces conditional computation into PEFT by organizing prompts, adapters, or LoRA modules as routed experts ( Dou et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2024a ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024 ) . However, these methods are predominantly validated on dense models. It therefore remains unclear how PEFT should interact with the existing experts and routers of an MoE model. In this paper, we systematically study adaptation position, expert granularity, update form, and load balancing to derive principled guidelines for applying PEFT to MoE models. Figure 1: Illustration of Position, PEFT Methods, and Auxiliary Loss.

sections.heading: PEFT for MoE architecture models.
sections.text: PEFT for pretrained MoE models is not a straightforward extension of dense-model PEFT, because sparse routing governs how limited trainable parameters receive supervision. Since each token is dispatched to a few experts, PEFT modules receive uneven, task-dependent signals, making expert selection and update sharing central design choices ( Wang et al., 2024c ) . Conventional top- k k routing also provides incomplete gradients for PEFT modules optimization during post-training ( Yao et al., ) . Moreover, load-balancing objectives may enforce overly uniform routing and weaken the specialization induced by expert-specific updates on narrow downstream distributions ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . Existing PEFT studies address parts of this through task-relevant expert selection, expert-wise allocation, joint router–expert adaptation, or additional routed adaptation modules ( Wang et al., 2024c ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . However, they often vary simultaneously in adaptation position, expert granularity, update form, routing strategy, and balancing objective, making it difficult to determine which choices consistently benefit. We therefore conduct a controlled study of these factors to derive robust principles for MoE adaptation.

sections.heading: 3.2 Study Design
sections.text: We evaluate Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, Gemma-4-26B-A4B, and GPT-OSS-20B on two complementary downstream tasks, specifically mathematical reasoning and intent classification. Appendix E details their architectures. For the intent classification task, the models are trained on ESFT_Intent ( Wang et al., 2024c ) and evaluated by exact match on 500 held-out examples. For the mathematical reasoning task, models are trained on MetaMathQA-R1, derived from MetaMathQA ( Yu et al., 2024 ) , and evaluated on MATH-500 ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) . We use MMLU-Pro ( Wang et al., 2024b ) and IFEval ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) to measure the general capabilities, including knowledge-based reasoning and instruction-following retained after downstream adaptation. For each configuration and model–task pair in the four design studies, we train three seeds per candidate learning rate and select the rate with the highest mean downstream score. We evaluate the three checkpoints at that rate on MMLU-Pro and IFEval and report three-seed means, without using general scores for selection. Detailed implementation settings are provided in Appendix B . Selected learning rates and Qwen3 training throughput are reported in Appendix H .

sections.heading: 4.1 Which Modules Should be Targeted for Adaptation?
sections.text: We compare attention-only ( r = 64 r=64 ), expert-only ( r = 256 r=256 ), and attention+experts ( r = 32 r=32 and 128 128 ) under a comparable budget, using one shared branch for the expert block to keep the focus on position. We repeat each with a rank-8 router update and also test the higher-budget attention/expert pair ( r = 64 / 256 r=64/256 ), with and without router adaptation. Figure 3: Visualized results of the study of adapted modules. Attn denotes attention, and gray labels report trainable parameters. Figure 3 summarizes the adaptation-position study. Expert-only adaptation leads across the six model–task cells at 68.6%, ahead of experts+router at 68.1% and attention+experts at 67.0%. It changes MMLU-Pro and IFEval by − 3.3 -3.3 and − 3.6 -3.6 points. Attention-only reaches 61.7%, with changes of − 10.4 -10.4 and − 7.9 -7.9 points. Attention+experts changes the two benchmarks by − 1.8 -1.8 and − 1.0 -1.0 points, while experts+router changes them by − 2.0 -2.0 and − 3.6 -3.6 points. Without and with router adaptation, the higher-budget settings reach 64.8% and 64.9%; MMLU-Pro changes by − 2.2 -2.2 and − 0.6 -0.6 points, and IFEval by − 2.4 -2.4 and − 1.0 -1.0 points. Expert-only is strongest at comparable budget, while attention+experts retains more general capability. Insight 1. For MoE fine-tuning, target the experts by default, and adapt the router only when the task calls for routing specialization.

sections.heading: 4.2 Which Granularity Should be Used to Adapt MoE Modules?
sections.text: Figure 2 contrasts a rank-256 module-level bypass, a rank-2 expert-level bypass, and weight-level updates at ranks 1 and 2. Figure 4: Visualized results of the study of MoE adaptation granularity. Figure 4 shows weight-level adaptation leading at rank 2 with 69.1%, followed by rank 1 at 68.5%, module-level bypass at 68.4%, and expert-level bypass at 64.7%. Rank 1 has the strongest general-capability profile, changing MMLU-Pro and IFEval by + 0.8 +0.8 and − 1.4 -1.4 points; rank 2 changes them by − 0.9 -0.9 and − 3.4 -3.4 . Both bypass alternatives reduce both benchmarks. Rank 2 gains 0.6 downstream points at roughly twice the trainable-parameter count. Insight 2. Weight-level adaptation provides the best trade-off. Rank- 1 1 is a strong default, achieving near-optimal downstream performance while preserving general capabilities. Increasing the rank brings only marginal gains, whereas bypass-based adaptation is generally less stable and less effective.

sections.heading: 4.3 Which PEFT Method Generally Works Best for Adapting MoE Models?
sections.text: We compare LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , DoRA ( Liu et al., 2024a ) , OFT ( Qiu et al., 2024 ) , FourierFT ( Gao et al., 2024b ) , and IA3 ( Liu et al., 2022 ) , alongside expert-level LoRA, MoE-LoRA ( Luo et al., 2024 ) , module-level LoRA, DAS-LoRA ( Tang et al., 2026 ) , and last-layer partial fine-tuning ( Ye et al., 2023 ) . Figure 5: Visualized results of the study of PEFT methods. Weight-level LoRA and DoRA tie at 68.5% across the six downstream cells. Both raise MMLU-Pro by 0.8 points; DoRA changes IFEval by -1.1, compared with -1.4 for LoRA. Among MoE-specific variants, layer-level LoRA leads at 66.7%, followed by MoE-LoRA at 65.7%, DAS-LoRA at 64.8%, and expert-level LoRA at 64.7%. OFT, FourierFT, IA3, and partial fine-tuning reach 60.8%, 43.6%, 41.3%, and 39.4%. Weight-level LoRA and DoRA provide the strongest downstream accuracy, with DoRA retaining more IFEval performance. Insight 3. Start expert-weight adaptation with standard LoRA or DoRA. Favor DoRA when preserving instruction-following performance is a priority.

sections.heading: 4.4 How Strong Should the Auxiliary Loss Coefficient Be Set For Adapting MoE Models?
sections.text: We vary the auxiliary loss coefficient from zero to 10 − 1 10^{-1} while holding the adaptation method and trainable-parameter count fixed, as illustrated in Figure 6 . Figure 6: Visualized results of the study of the strength of auxiliary loss. Figure 6 shows a 68.5% downstream average without auxiliary loss; coefficients of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , 10 − 3 10^{-3} , 10 − 2 10^{-2} , and 10 − 1 10^{-1} yield 68.1%, 66.8%, 64.6%, and 58.6%. At 10 − 3 10^{-3} , MMLU-Pro rises 1.2 points, IFEval falls 2.5, and the downstream average falls 1.7 relative to zero. At 10 − 1 10^{-1} , MMLU-Pro and IFEval fall 0.9 and 8.5 points. Larger coefficients therefore reduce downstream performance and IFEval retention. Insight 4. The auxiliary loss should be disabled or assigned a very small coefficient during MoE adaptation. A coefficient around 10 − 4 10^{-4} is a safe choice when routing regularization is required, whereas larger values can substantially degrade downstream performance.

sections.heading: 5 Design Implications
sections.text: To test whether the insights transfer to a composite method, we refine MoE 2 -LoRA ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . It follows Insight 1 by adapting only MoE modules with frozen attention and follows Insight 4 by disabling auxiliary load balancing. It also uses the native router to select entries from a shared pool without updating router weights. Its remaining mismatch is Insight 2: the pool is a module-level bypass rather than an update to native expert projections. We therefore replace each of the 128 rank-32 pool entries with a low-rank update to native expert weights while retaining the routed pool, router-driven selection, frozen attention, and zero balancing coefficient. sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: MoE-PEFT is not only a choice of update parameterization; placement, granularity, optimization, and routing objectives materially change its reliability. Across three backbones and two tasks, expert FFNs are the downstream-robust placement, native expert weights are the most reliable evaluated granularity, LoRA/DoRA lead when a high downstream floor is enforced, and zero auxiliary load balancing is the only no-tuning joint default. None is universal: mixed placement can drift less, low-drift update forms can adapt poorly, and a moderate auxiliary coefficient can trade downstream accuracy for better retention of some general capabilities. Our Qwen3 analyses show that weight-level adaptation combines broad functional responses with strong reuse of pretrained spectral structure. These defaults also carry over beyond our own grid: a weight-level redesign of MoE 2 -LoRA that moves its module-level bypass pool into native expert weights improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters at a small downstream cost. We therefore offer these defaults as a scoped but directionally reliable starting point for MoE adaptation. We hope our findings and analyses can stimulate further research on parameter-efficient adaptation of MoE models, and encourage future methods to report what each design choice costs the pretrained model alongside what it gains.

The adapted weight is W ′ = Diag ⁡ ( m ⊘ ∥ V ∥ row ) ​ V . W^{\prime}=\operatorname{Diag}\!\left(m\oslash\lVert V\rVert_{\mathrm{row}}\right)V. (17) Here ⊘ \oslash denotes elementwise division. This row-wise expression is the transpose-equivalent form of the column-wise normalization used in the original DoRA notation. (18) The stop-gradient operation changes the backward graph, not the numerical forward value. sections.text: FourierFT ( Gao et al., 2024b ) represents a dense weight update using a small number of trainable Fourier coefficients. Let Ω \Omega be a fixed random support in the two-dimensional frequency domain, and let S Ω ​ ( c ) S_{\Omega}(c) scatter the trainable real coefficient vector c c into the corresponding frequency locations. The update is Δ ​ W = γ ​ Re ⁡ [ IDFT 2 ⁡ ( S Ω ​ ( c ) ) ] , W ′ = W + Δ ​ W . \Delta W=\gamma\,\operatorname{Re}\!\left[\operatorname{IDFT}_{2}\!\left(S_{\Omega}(c)\right)\right],\qquad W^{\prime}=W+\Delta W. (22) The original method samples the support once and uses randomly initialized coefficients. In our benchmark implementation, the support is fixed with seed 2024, the coefficients are instead initialized to zero so that Δ ​ W = 0 \Delta W=0 initially, and the update scale is set to γ = 150 \gamma=150 . sections.heading: B.1 Downstream and General-Capability Evaluation
sections.text: The mathematical-reasoning experiments fine-tune on MetaMathQA-R1 (huggingface oumi-ai/MetaMathQA-R1 ), a pre-constructed synthetic dataset whose problems are drawn from MetaMathQA ( Yu et al., 2024 ) and whose responses are generated by DeepSeek-R1. We use only the final solution portion of each response for training, excluding the intermediate think content. Mathematical reasoning is evaluated on the 500 examples in MATH-500 ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) . The intent experiments fine-tune on ESFT_Intent and report exact-match accuracy on a held-out set of 500 examples. We assess general-capability retention on MMLU-Pro ( Wang et al., 2024b ) and IFEval ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) . For each model–task–configuration in the four design studies, we train every candidate learning rate with three random seeds and select one rate by mean downstream score. We then evaluate the three checkpoints at that rate on MMLU-Pro and IFEval. Downstream and general-capability scores are averaged over the same three seeds; general scores do not affect learning-rate selection. sections.heading: B.2 Common Optimization Settings
sections.text: All reported fine-tuning runs use four GPUs, BF16 computation, gradient checkpointing, and DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 ( Rasley et al., 2020 ) . Optimization uses fused AdamW with β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 , and ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} ; the learning-rate schedule is cosine with a 0.1 warmup ratio. For every experiment, the learning rate is selected by grid search over candidates drawn from { 10 − 5 , 10 − 4 , 10 − 3 } \{10^{-5},10^{-4},10^{-3}\} . No adapter dropout was configured. All backbones are loaded with remote model code enabled. The per-device batch size is 6 with six accumulation steps on four GPUs, giving an effective batch size of 6 × 6 × 4 = 144 6\times 6\times 4=144 . Gemma-4 Intent uses a per-device batch size of 4 and nine accumulation steps, preserving the same effective batch size of 4 × 9 × 4 = 144 4\times 9\times 4=144 . GPT-OSS Intent explicitly disables FlashAttention.

sections.heading: Adaptation position.
sections.text: Starting from the experts-only reference, adding attention adaptation at an effectively matched parameter budget consistently weakens downstream performance: Intent decreases from 84.00 to 81.60 and MATH-500 from 60.00 to 56.60. For each task, the joint Attention+experts configuration also degrades at least one upstream benchmark. On Intent, IFEval falls from 18.11 to 14.23 despite the MMLU-Pro improvement; on Math, MMLU-Pro falls from 48.19 to 47.56 despite the IFEval improvement. Adding attention therefore fails to provide a consistent benefit and instead introduces simultaneous downstream and upstream degradation on both tasks. These results reinforce Insight 1: for MoE fine-tuning, target the experts by default and unfreeze shared attention modules cautiously, since adapting more modules does not necessarily yield better transfer and may amplify general-capability forgetting.

sections.heading: Auxiliary load balancing.
sections.text: On Intent, the smallest coefficient, 10 − 4 10^{-4} , remains competitive: it improves Intent from 84.00 to 85.00 and MMLU-Pro from 45.26 to 47.46, with only a 0.55-point decrease on IFEval. This local benefit does not transfer to Math, where the same coefficient reduces MATH-500 from 60.00 to 56.40 and MMLU-Pro from 48.19 to 47.27, although IFEval improves. The other nonzero coefficients are generally more damaging. They all lower downstream performance on both tasks; on Intent, the larger coefficients also cause substantial upstream degradation, while on Math the IFEval gains are consistently accompanied by losses on both MATH-500 and MMLU-Pro. Thus, auxiliary balancing does not yield a task-stable improvement. These results support Insight 4: the auxiliary loss should be disabled or assigned a very small coefficient during MoE adaptation. A coefficient around 10 − 4 10^{-4} is a safe choice when routing regularization is required and may benefit particular datasets, whereas larger values can substantially degrade downstream performance.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.26370v1 [cs.LG] 19 Oct 2026 An Empirical Study of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Minglei Li 1 * Peng Ye 2,3 * Haonan He 2,4 Jingqi Ye 2,4 Qingyu Yang 2,5 Tao Chen 1,6 † \dagger Affiliation: 1 Fudan University 2 Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory 3 The Chinese University of Hong Kong 4 University of Science and Technology of China 5 KTH Royal Institute of Technology 6 Shanghai Innovation Institute Abstract Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods are critical for adapting large models under resource-constrained settings. However, as mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, which offer efficient inference at massive parameter scales, gain increasing prevalence in the community, a critical gap arising from the lack of systematic recipes for applying PEFT to MoE models. To narrow this gap, we conduct a large-scale systematic study that investigates a set of essential design recipes, including which modules should be adapted, which granularity should be used to adapt MoE modules, which PEFT method to use, and to what extent should the load-balancing objective be used, across three MoE backbones on downstream tasks and general knowledge tasks. Our experiments yield several key insights. First, adapting MoE experts alone achieves the highest downstream performance with competitive general capability retention under a comparable parameter budget. Second, native expert-weight updates offer a better downstream–retention trade-off than adapters that bypass experts or entire MoE modules. Third, LoRA and DoRA together define the strongest operating region for high downstream accuracy among the evaluated PEFT methods. Fourth, no nonzero load-balancing coefficient Pareto-dominates the zero baseline. We finally evaluate a weight-level redesign of MoE 2 -LoRA on Qwen3. Moving its module-level bypass pool into native expert weights improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters and a 3.2-point average downstream cost. 1 Introduction Mixture-of-experts architectures ( Shazeer et al., 2017 ; Lepikhin et al., 2021 ; Fedus et al., 2022 ; Du et al., 2022 ) enable extensive scaling of model parameters while activating only a small fraction of parameters per input unit. This sparse activation paradigm offers an outstanding trade-off between performance and computation, and has consequently been adopted by frontier models such as GLM-5.2 ( GLM-5 Team, 2026 ) and Kimi-K3 ( Kimi Team, 2026 ) . Despite the increasing prevalence of MoE architectures, most existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Houlsby et al., 2019 ; Li and Liang, 2021 ) and recipes were originally designed for dense models, and the community still lacks a systematic guideline for applying PEFT methods to MoE structures. Given that MoE models typically comprise a massive number of parameters, it is essential to adopt a scientifically grounded guideline for applying PEFT to such models to achieve efficient adaptation. This gap therefore raises a pressing question: How can we adapt MoE models to achieve the best performance-efficiency balance with the least forgetting? To answer this question, we conduct a large-scale systematic empirical study using representative MoE backbones from different families, including Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) , Gemma-4-26B-A4B ( Gemma Team, 2026 ) , and GPT-OSS-20B ( OpenAI, 2025 ) . Specifically, we structure our study around four main axes: (1) which modules should be targeted for adapting MoE models under a similar trainable parameter budget? (2) should adaptation granularity for MoE modules be set at the module level, expert level, or weight level? (3) which PEFT method generally works best for adapting MoE models? (4) how strong should the auxiliary loss coefficient be set for adapting MoE models? We conduct the study using two distinct downstream tasks and two general tasks. The first downstream task is mathematical reasoning, on which base models typically already possess strong capabilities; it serves to probe whether further leverages well-established knowledge. The second downstream task is an intent classification task, which yields unsatisfactory results for the three base models and therefore provides a more stringent test of a PEFT method’s ability to adapt in under-represented regimes. Our study therefore yields four instructive insights: (1) applying adaptation solely to experts, achieves the best downstream performance; (2) within the MoE modules, applying adaptation at the weight level is more reliable than at the expert level or module level; (3) among the evaluated PEFT methods, LoRA and DoRA deliver the strongest downstream performance, whereas methods with weaker general capabilities retention can fail to learn the target task properly; (4) auxiliary load balancing may degrade performance on both downstream tasks and general capabilities retention. Guided by these findings, we revisit MoE 2 -LoRA, a PEFT method tailred for MoE fine-tuning, which established a learned mapping between the selection of pre-trained MoE experts and that of LoRA experts. Our modification on MoE 2 -LoRA improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters and only a 3.2-point average downstream cost, turning a large task-dependent forgetting into near-complete retention and thereby showing that our insights are effective beyond the controlled grid. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • To our knowledge, this is the first large-scale PEFT study conducted directly on pretrained MoE LLMs, covering four design axes, three heterogeneous backbones, and two downstream tasks. Beyond the downstream accuracy that PEFT work usually reports alone, we pair every selected checkpoint with general-capability evaluation on MMLU-Pro and IFEval, so each design choice is judged by what it gains and by what it costs the pretrained model. • We distill the study into four actionable insights on adaptation position, expert granularity, update form, and load balancing, each stated with the regime in which it holds, providing concrete defaults and open questions for future work on MoE adaptation. Functional and spectral analyses explain how weight-level updates reuse pretrained expert computation. • We show the insights are practical by refining MoE 2 -LoRA, a recent routed-pool method, along the single axis it does not already follow, which improves all four general-capability endpoints with 17% fewer parameters. 2 Related Work Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning (PEFT). PEFT adapts large models by learning a small set of parameters while keeping pretrained weights largely frozen. Low-rank methods modify pretrained weights through compact updates: LoRA learns a low-rank residual, while DoRA decouples weight magnitude and direction to improve the update ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2024a ) . OFT and FourierFT further restrict the update space through orthogonal transformations and frequency-domain parameterization, respectively ( Qiu et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2024b ) , whereas IA3 adapts the model by scaling intermediate activations ( Liu et al., 2022 ) . A complementary line introduces conditional computation into PEFT by organizing prompts, adapters, or LoRA modules as routed experts ( Dou et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2024a ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024 ) . However, these methods are predominantly validated on dense models. It therefore remains unclear how PEFT should interact with the existing experts and routers of an MoE model. In this paper, we systematically study adaptation position, expert granularity, update form, and load balancing to derive principled guidelines for applying PEFT to MoE models. Figure 1: Illustration of Position, PEFT Methods, and Auxiliary Loss. PEFT for MoE architecture models. PEFT for pretrained MoE models is not a straightforward extension of dense-model PEFT, because sparse routing governs how limited trainable parameters receive supervision. Since each token is dispatched to a few experts, PEFT modules receive uneven, task-dependent signals, making expert selection and update sharing central design choices ( Wang et al., 2024c ) . Conventional top- k k routing also provides incomplete gradients for PEFT modules optimization during post-training ( Yao et al., ) . Moreover, load-balancing objectives may enforce overly uniform routing and weaken the specialization induced by expert-specific updates on narrow downstream distributions ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . Existing PEFT studies address parts of this through task-relevant expert selection, expert-wise allocation, joint router–expert adaptation, or additional routed adaptation modules ( Wang et al., 2024c ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . However, they often vary simultaneously in adaptation position, expert granularity, update form, routing strategy, and balancing objective, making it difficult to determine which choices consistently benefit. We therefore conduct a controlled study of these factors to derive robust principles for MoE adaptation. 3 Background and Study Design 3.1 Background Figure 2: Three evaluated adaptation granularities of the MoE module. This work investigates the principled application of PEFT methods to MoE models, with an emphasis on the MoE modules. Formally, given a hidden state x x , the computation inside an MoE module can be written as y = ∑ e ∈ TopK ⁡ ( g ⁡ ( x ) ) p e ​ ( x ) ​ f e ​ ( x ) , y=\sum_{e\in\operatorname{TopK}(g(x))}p_{e}(x)\,f_{e}(x), (1) where g g denotes the router, p e p_{e} is the routing probability for expert e e , and f e f_{e} represents the transformation of expert e e . We model the fine-tuning process as an incremental update of the pre-trained weights: W ′ = W + Δ ​ W , W^{\prime}=W+\Delta W, (2) where W ′ ∈ ℝ d out × d in W^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} is the fine-tuned weight, and W W and Δ ​ W \Delta W correspond to the pre-trained weight and its additive update, respectively. In the case of LoRA, the update is parameterized as Δ ​ W = α r ​ B ​ A \Delta W=\frac{\alpha}{r}BA , with low-rank matrices A ∈ ℝ r × d in A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} and B ∈ ℝ d out × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times r} , while α \alpha and r r are hyper-parameters controlling the update scale and rank. Other PEFT methods evaluated in this study are deferred to Appendix A . 3.2 Study Design We evaluate Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, Gemma-4-26B-A4B, and GPT-OSS-20B on two complementary downstream tasks, specifically mathematical reasoning and intent classification. Appendix E details their architectures. For the intent classification task, the models are trained on ESFT_Intent ( Wang et al., 2024c ) and evaluated by exact match on 500 held-out examples. For the mathematical reasoning task, models are trained on MetaMathQA-R1, derived from MetaMathQA ( Yu et al., 2024 ) , and evaluated on MATH-500 ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) . We use MMLU-Pro ( Wang et al., 2024b ) and IFEval ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) to measure the general capabilities, including knowledge-based reasoning and instruction-following retained after downstream adaptation. For each configuration and model–task pair in the four design studies, we train three seeds per candidate learning rate and select the rate with the highest mean downstream score. We evaluate the three checkpoints at that rate on MMLU-Pro and IFEval and report three-seed means, without using general scores for selection. Detailed implementation settings are provided in Appendix B . Selected learning rates and Qwen3 training throughput are reported in Appendix H . 4 Empirical Study 4.1 Which Modules Should be Targeted for Adaptation? We compare attention-only ( r = 64 r=64 ), expert-only ( r = 256 r=256 ), and attention+experts ( r = 32 r=32 and 128 128 ) under a comparable budget, using one shared branch for the expert block to keep the focus on position. We repeat each with a rank-8 router update and also test the higher-budget attention/expert pair ( r = 64 / 256 r=64/256 ), with and without router adaptation. Figure 3: Visualized results of the study of adapted modules. Attn denotes attention, and gray labels report trainable parameters. Figure 3 summarizes the adaptation-position study. Expert-only adaptation leads across the six model–task cells at 68.6%, ahead of experts+router at 68.1% and attention+experts at 67.0%. It changes MMLU-Pro and IFEval by − 3.3 -3.3 and − 3.6 -3.6 points. Attention-only reaches 61.7%, with changes of − 10.4 -10.4 and − 7.9 -7.9 points. Attention+experts changes the two benchmarks by − 1.8 -1.8 and − 1.0 -1.0 points, while experts+router changes them by − 2.0 -2.0 and − 3.6 -3.6 points. Without and with router adaptation, the higher-budget settings reach 64.8% and 64.9%; MMLU-Pro changes by − 2.2 -2.2 and − 0.6 -0.6 points, and IFEval by − 2.4 -2.4 and − 1.0 -1.0 points. Expert-only is strongest at comparable budget, while attention+experts retains more general capability. Insight 1. For MoE fine-tuning, target the experts by default, and adapt the router only when the task calls for routing specialization. 4.2 Which Granularity Should be Used to Adapt MoE Modules? Figure 2 contrasts a rank-256 module-level bypass, a rank-2 expert-level bypass, and weight-level updates at ranks 1 and 2. Figure 4: Visualized results of the study of MoE adaptation granularity. Figure 4 shows weight-level adaptation leading at rank 2 with 69.1%, followed by rank 1 at 68.5%, module-level bypass at 68.4%, and expert-level bypass at 64.7%. Rank 1 has the strongest general-capability profile, changing MMLU-Pro and IFEval by + 0.8 +0.8 and − 1.4 -1.4 points; rank 2 changes them by − 0.9 -0.9 and − 3.4 -3.4 . Both bypass alternatives reduce both benchmarks. Rank 2 gains 0.6 downstream points at roughly twice the trainable-parameter count. Insight 2. Weight-level adaptation provides the best trade-off. Rank- 1 1 is a strong default, achieving near-optimal downstream performance while preserving general capabilities. Increasing the rank brings only marginal gains, whereas bypass-based adaptation is generally less stable and less effective. 4.3 Which PEFT Method Generally Works Best for Adapting MoE Models? We compare LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , DoRA ( Liu et al., 2024a ) , OFT ( Qiu et al., 2024 ) , FourierFT ( Gao et al., 2024b ) , and IA3 ( Liu et al., 2022 ) , alongside expert-level LoRA, MoE-LoRA ( Luo et al., 2024 ) , module-level LoRA, DAS-LoRA ( Tang et al., 2026 ) , and last-layer partial fine-tuning ( Ye et al., 2023 ) . Figure 5: Visualized results of the study of PEFT methods. Weight-level LoRA and DoRA tie at 68.5% across the six downstream cells. Both raise MMLU-Pro by 0.8 points; DoRA changes IFEval by -1.1, compared with -1.4 for LoRA. Among MoE-specific variants, layer-level LoRA leads at 66.7%, followed by MoE-LoRA at 65.7%, DAS-LoRA at 64.8%, and expert-level LoRA at 64.7%. OFT, FourierFT, IA3, and partial fine-tuning reach 60.8%, 43.6%, 41.3%, and 39.4%. Weight-level LoRA and DoRA provide the strongest downstream accuracy, with DoRA retaining more IFEval performance. Insight 3. Start expert-weight adaptation with standard LoRA or DoRA. Favor DoRA when preserving instruction-following performance is a priority. 4.4 How Strong Should the Auxiliary Loss Coefficient Be Set For Adapting MoE Models? We vary the auxiliary loss coefficient from zero to 10 − 1 10^{-1} while holding the adaptation method and trainable-parameter count fixed, as illustrated in Figure 6 . Figure 6: Visualized results of the study of the strength of auxiliary loss. Figure 6 shows a 68.5% downstream average without auxiliary loss; coefficients of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , 10 − 3 10^{-3} , 10 − 2 10^{-2} , and 10 − 1 10^{-1} yield 68.1%, 66.8%, 64.6%, and 58.6%. At 10 − 3 10^{-3} , MMLU-Pro rises 1.2 points, IFEval falls 2.5, and the downstream average falls 1.7 relative to zero. At 10 − 1 10^{-1} , MMLU-Pro and IFEval fall 0.9 and 8.5 points. Larger coefficients therefore reduce downstream performance and IFEval retention. Insight 4. The auxiliary loss should be disabled or assigned a very small coefficient during MoE adaptation. A coefficient around 10 − 4 10^{-4} is a safe choice when routing regularization is required, whereas larger values can substantially degrade downstream performance. 5 Design Implications To test whether the insights transfer to a composite method, we refine MoE 2 -LoRA ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . It follows Insight 1 by adapting only MoE modules with frozen attention and follows Insight 4 by disabling auxiliary load balancing. It also uses the native router to select entries from a shared pool without updating router weights. Its remaining mismatch is Insight 2: the pool is a module-level bypass rather than an update to native expert projections. We therefore replace each of the 128 rank-32 pool entries with a low-rank update to native expert weights while retaining the routed pool, router-driven selection, frozen attention, and zero balancing coefficient. Appendix A.1 gives both update equations. Table 1 shows this change reduces the parameter count by 17.0%, from 47.71M to 39.58M. It improves MMLU-Pro and IFEval by 2.44 and 5.18 points on Math, and by 5.94 and 17.93 points on Intent. Figure 7 shows mean effective ranks of 63.90 and 69.08 for weight-level r = 1 r=1 on Math and Intent, compared with 16.31 and 15.91 for expert-level r = 2 r=2 . Figure 8: Pretrained spectral consistency on Qwen3: Math and Intent energy profiles and score distributions across layer–expert positions. Weight-level updates follow the pretrained spectrum. Figure 8 shows mean C spec C_{\mathrm{spec}} values of 0.812 0.812 and 0.822 0.822 on Math and 0.733 0.733 and 0.741 0.741 on Intent for weight-level ranks 1 and 2, versus 0.141 0.141 and 0.087 0.087 for expert-level rank 2. Rank-one weight updates lead across all 48 layer means and at 99.8% of Math and 96.3% of Intent positions. Measurements across gate, up, and down projections confirm spectral alignment; rank two broadens responses while retaining it. These results explain the low-rank efficiency behind Insight 2. 7 Conclusion MoE-PEFT is not only a choice of update parameterization; placement, granularity, optimization, and routing objectives materially change its reliability. Across three backbones and two tasks, expert FFNs are the downstream-robust placement, native expert weights are the most reliable evaluated granularity, LoRA/DoRA lead when a high downstream floor is enforced, and zero auxiliary load balancing is the only no-tuning joint default. None is universal: mixed placement can drift less, low-drift update forms can adapt poorly, and a moderate auxiliary coefficient can trade downstream accuracy for better retention of some general capabilities. Our Qwen3 analyses show that weight-level adaptation combines broad functional responses with strong reuse of pretrained spectral structure. These defaults also carry over beyond our own grid: a weight-level redesign of MoE 2 -LoRA that moves its module-level bypass pool into native expert weights improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters at a small downstream cost. We therefore offer these defaults as a scoped but directionally reliable starting point for MoE adaptation. We hope our findings and analyses can stimulate further research on parameter-efficient adaptation of MoE models, and encourage future methods to report what each design choice costs the pretrained model alongside what it gains.
